identification.summary: Iran-based cyber-espionage cluster that Microsoft tracked as DEV-0228 and now calls Cuboid Sandstorm [S1][S2]. In July 2021 it compromised a single Israel-based IT company that provides business management software. It then used that company's credentials and access to reach downstream customers in Israel's defense, energy and legal sectors [S1][S3]. Microsoft says the group compromised at least a dozen other organizations and assesses that at least four were reached with the stolen IT-provider access [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: July 2021 (credential dumping at the Israeli IT provider in early July 2021) [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Cuboid Sandstorm (formerly DEV-0228) [S2]. When Microsoft published its 2021 report, a DEV designation marked a cluster whose origin or identity was not yet established with high confidence [S1]. Microsoft's mapping also lists IMPERIAL KITTEN (CrowdStrike) for Cuboid Sandstorm, but the same file lists IMPERIAL KITTEN under Crimson Sandstorm and Smoke Sandstorm as well, so that alias is a many-to-one overlap rather than an equivalence [S2]. Cybereason's MalKamak / ShellClient reporting has tooling similarities but is a separate vendor cluster (see gaps) [S4][S8]. No MITRE ATT&CK group ID is recorded.

attribution.sponsor: Iran. Microsoft assesses the cluster as based in Iran and treats the activity as part of a broader Iranian espionage effort against organizations of interest to the Iranian regime [S1]. No specific Iranian organization is named for Cuboid Sandstorm in the sources gathered.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft (MSTIC) assessment: based in Iran [S1]. In 2021 the DEV label meant Microsoft had not yet reached high confidence on origin or identity. No government attribution was found for this cluster. Microsoft maps the CrowdStrike name IMPERIAL KITTEN to three Sandstorm actors [S2], so CrowdStrike assessments of that cluster should not be applied to Cuboid Sandstorm specifically.
attribution.basis: Microsoft incident telemetry, nation-state notifications and tool hashes [S1]; Microsoft naming mapping [S2].

objectives: Espionage against Israeli organizations of interest to the Iranian regime, achieved by compromising a trusted IT service provider and pivoting to its customers [S1]. Microsoft frames the wider 2021 Iranian IT-sector targeting as an effort to gain indirect access to IT providers' clients and subsidiaries [S1].

sectors: IT services / business management software providers [S1]
targeting.notes: All victims named for DEV-0228 are in Israel [S1]. Microsoft's report also covers wider Iranian activity against IT companies in India and the UAE, and covers DEV-0056 in Bahrain. Those findings belong to the broader Iranian set or to DEV-0056 (now Smoke Sandstorm), not to Cuboid Sandstorm specifically [S1].

capabilities.summary: Microsoft describes a supply-chain style pivot. The group dumped credentials on the IT provider's on-premises network, then reused the provider's accounts to reach customers. It used PAExec for remote execution against a law firm, and an email account the IT provider had in a defense company's Office 365 tenant [S1]. Its custom .NET remote access trojan used Dropbox for command and control and was disguised as RuntimeBroker.exe or svchost.exe. Microsoft Defender detects it as Backdoor:MSIL/ShellClient.A [S1]. After gaining persistence, the operators dumped LSASS memory. They staged lsa.exe, PAExec (pa.exe), ProcDump (pc.exe) and Rar.exe in C:\Windows\TAPI. Mimikatz-related detections were also reported [S1]. Microsoft did not publish C2 IP addresses or domains [S1].

campaigns.name: Israeli IT provider compromise
campaigns.summary: DEV-0228 compromised an Israel-based business-management software provider and dumped credentials from its on-premises network in early July 2021.

campaigns.name: Downstream customer intrusions
campaigns.summary: Using the provider's access, the group compromised at least a dozen other organizations. These included an Israeli law firm in August, reached via PAExec, and an Israeli defense company reached through the provider's Office 365 account. Defense, energy and legal sectors were affected.

campaigns.name: Microsoft public disclosure
campaigns.summary: Microsoft published DEV-0228 activity, tool hashes, Defender detections and hunting queries as part of its report on rising Iranian targeting of the IT sector.

diamond.adversary: An Iran-based espionage cluster (Microsoft assessment). No named organization or individuals are given [S1].
diamond.capability: Credential dumping (LSASS, ProcDump, a custom lsa.exe); PAExec lateral movement; a custom .NET RAT detected as ShellClient that uses Dropbox C2; RAR staging [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: The Dropbox cloud service used as C2; reused IT-provider accounts and an Office 365 tenant account as access paths. No dedicated C2 domains or IPs were published [S1].
diamond.victim: An Israeli business-management software/IT provider and its downstream customers in Israeli defense, energy and legal sectors [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Iranian regime intelligence interest in Israeli defense, energy and legal organizations, pursued through trusted third parties [S1].
diamond.technology: Trusted IT-provider relationships: shared credentials, provider-managed accounts, and provider accounts inside customer Office 365 tenants. Also abuse of legitimate cloud storage for C2 [S1].

gaps: Alias ambiguity: Microsoft's mapping lists IMPERIAL KITTEN under Cuboid, Crimson and Smoke Sandstorm, so CrowdStrike's IMPERIAL KITTEN reporting cannot be assigned to Cuboid Sandstorm from the sources gathered [S2].

Possible overlap with Cybereason's MalKamak (Operation GhostShell). Cybereason's ShellClient RAT also used Dropbox C2 and ran as svchost.exe with the internal name RuntimeBroker.exe. It was first found in a July 2021 incident, and reporting also mentions an lsa.exe credential dumper. Microsoft's DEV-0228 detection is named ShellClient. However, no source gathered explicitly equates DEV-0228/Cuboid Sandstorm with MalKamak. MalKamak victims were aerospace and telecom firms, mainly in the Middle East with others in the US, Russia and Europe [S1][S4][S8].
No public Cuboid Sandstorm activity after the November 2021 disclosure was found. Current operational status is unknown.
The sponsoring Iranian organization (MOIS, IRGC or a contractor) is not stated by Microsoft.
The identities of the Israeli IT provider and the downstream victims are not public.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key terrain includes IT and managed-service providers with standing credentials or tenant accounts in defense and energy customers [S1]. STEP 2 (effects): Trusted-provider access can bypass perimeter controls on the end target. Abuse of Dropbox C2 blends with sanctioned cloud traffic [S1]. STEP 3 (threat model): Compromise a provider, dump credentials (LSASS/ProcDump), reuse provider accounts, move laterally with PAExec, plant a Dropbox-C2 RAT disguised as svchost.exe or RuntimeBroker.exe, and stage data with RAR [S1]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is espionage against Israeli or partner defense and energy organizations through a shared IT vendor. MDCOA is the same pivot technique applied to a vendor that supports US or coalition defense contractors, giving broad covert access across multiple customers. Candidate indicators: files created in C:\Windows\TAPI; PAExec execution; Defender detections Backdoor:MSIL/ShellClient.A or Mimikatz; LSASS access by unusual processes; svchost.exe or RuntimeBroker.exe running from non-standard paths and calling Dropbox APIs; provider-provisioned O365 accounts logging in from anonymizing services [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: Track third-party and MSP accounts that hold access into DoD-adjacent and DIB tenants. Cuboid Sandstorm's documented path ran through a provider's O365 account in a defense company [S1]. (2) Authorities: Defending contractor and provider networks generally falls to the owners plus DC3 and DIB coordination rather than DoD cyber forces directly. Pre-coordinate information sharing. (3) Mission assurance: Enforce MFA and conditional access on vendor accounts, block ActiveSync bypass, and enable the ASR rule against LSASS credential theft, following Microsoft's mitigations [S1]. (4) Coordination: Share IOCs with coalition partners, especially Israel. Alias overlap (IMPERIAL KITTEN mapped to three Microsoft actors) means cross-vendor reporting must be deconflicted before it drives attribution-based decisions [S2].
